nodes.label: CrySLDoc
nodes.rationale: A batch documentation compiler turning formal CrySL rules into a static HTML site explaining secure Java crypto API usage to developers who do not know CrySL syntax. Successor to CogniCrypt's original template-based generator (2021-2024, Ritika Singh / Sven Feldmann); Roshan Samantaray added the Python LLM sidecar, dual OpenAI/gateway backends and RAG grounding in 2025-2026.
nodes.author: Roshan Samantaray
nodes.contributor: Ritika Singh, Sven Feldmann, Michael Schlichtig, André Sonntag

nodes.label: Three-tier filesystem-coupled architecture
nodes.rationale: Three tiers connected only by the filesystem and OS process boundaries, with no in-process coupling between Java and Python. The Java side spawns Python via ProcessBuilder and communicates through JSON files and plain .txt caches, which keeps the LLM layer entirely optional and the deterministic pipeline runnable with no Python at all.

nodes.label: ComposedRule - the central DTO
nodes.rationale: A 24-field DTO with no logic that every subsystem writes into and FreeMarker reads from exclusively - the contract between rule analysis, LLM generation and HTML rendering. Its string fields already contain HTML markup produced by the sentence generators, which templates render unescaped and which is also forwarded verbatim into LLM prompts.

nodes.label: The twelve sentence generators
nodes.rationale: ClassEventForb, Order, Ensures, EnsuresCaseTwo, Negates, ConstraintsComparison, ConstraintsVc, ConstraintsPred, ConstraintCrySLVC, ConstraintCryslnocallto, ConstraintCrySLInstanceof and ConstraintCrySLandencmode turn a parsed CrySLRule plus Templates/* fragments into English sentences carrying embedded HTML. About 4,600 lines - the actual product - with zero test coverage, and where nearly every High-severity audit finding lived.

nodes.label: The 51 bundled CrySL rules
nodes.rationale: Vendored copies of JavaCryptographicArchitecture:3.1.1:ruleset, byte-identical to the Maven artifact except CRLF endings in three files - which is why the Maven unpack-ruleset step is dead. Order.java re-parses the raw text rather than the parsed object model to recover event labels and the ORDER regex for prose generation.

nodes.label: Predicate dependency ordering and graph sanitization
nodes.rationale: Provider/consumer graphs are sanitized per rule (self-loop removal, reachability restriction, Tarjan SCC collapse), verified by GraphVerification as a production assertion that throws IllegalStateException, then topologically ordered leaf-to-root with Kahn's algorithm. PredicateTreeGenerator builds the requires/ensures trees the UI renders.

nodes.label: LLM explanation generation flow
nodes.rationale: Per rule x four languages, up to 204 subprocess spawns. Java serialises ComposedRule fields via Gson, sanitizes into llm/sanitized_rules/, and spawns Python, which re-reads the raw .crysl, loads depth-1 cycle-safe dependency context from sibling sanitized JSONs, optionally retrieves six RAG chunks, and issues one completion at temperature 0.3 against a prompt requiring eight exact markdown headings and forbidding raw CrySL notation.

nodes.label: Secure example generation flow
nodes.rationale: The most elaborate feature: a size-shaped authoritative CrySL contract with a drop-priority order, a cached CrySL primer from the paper index, a temperature-0.0 prompt with a strict compilation contract plus 13 lettered security guardrails, deterministic post-patching of known model mistakes, then compile-and-repair for up to CRYSLDOC_MAX_REPAIRS rounds. If still failing it raises rather than emit broken code, and Java records a typed placeholder the next run retries.

nodes.label: Insecure example generation flow
nodes.rationale: Deliberately minimal by contrast with the secure path: a single temperature-0.3 prompt asking the model to violate the rule while staying syntactically valid, with no compile check, no patching and no repair loop. It also interpolates ComposedRule fields including their embedded HTML markup directly into the prompt.

nodes.label: javac compile gate for secure examples
nodes.rationale: The single safety property the whole secure-example design rests on. Now defaults to the JDK alone so it tests what actually matters - that a reader with a plain JDK can compile the published example - with the full runtime classpath opt-in behind CRYSLDOC_COMPILE_USE_RUNTIME_CLASSPATH and specific jars addable via CRYSLDOC_COMPILE_CLASSPATH, which is how javax.servlet.http.Cookie is handled.

nodes.label: RAG index over the CrySL TSE'19 paper
nodes.rationale: tse19CrySL.pdf is the sole RAG corpus, chunked and embedded into a FAISS index cached under rag_cache/<provider>__<model>__<hash>/. Unlike the other caches this one is content-derived - keyed on sha256 of provider, model, absolute PDF path and size:mtime - and structurally revalidated on load, so it is the only cache layer that cannot go stale.

nodes.label: Dual backend - OpenAI and UPB AI-Gateway
nodes.rationale: --llm-backend fully determines which is used; no fallback between them occurs. Known asymmetry: llm_writer_gateway.py threads GATEWAY_CHAT_MODEL/GATEWAY_EMB_MODEL into its shared CLI config while llm_writer.py passes neither, so OPENAI_CHAT_MODEL affects the code-example writers but is silently ignored by the explanation writer, which stays hardcoded to gpt-4o-mini.

nodes.label: Cross-process gateway RPM throttle
nodes.rationale: The only concurrency primitive in the repository: a JSON timestamp file guarded by fcntl.flock or msvcrt.locking with an atomic temp-file-rename write. It is correctly built for concurrent callers even though nothing in the pipeline calls it concurrently - it exists because the state file is process-durable, protecting against two separate crysldoc invocations racing.

nodes.label: Three-layer filesystem cache model
nodes.rationale: Explanations, code examples, RAG index and sanitized rule JSON, all filesystem-only with no database. Two caveats survive the placeholder fix: cache keys are the filename alone and carry no model or backend identifier, so switching backend or model silently serves the old model's text (use a distinct --reportPath per backend when comparing); and sanitized rule JSONs remain existence-gated and are never regenerated when the source .crysl changes.

nodes.label: Placeholder-aware cache invalidation
nodes.rationale: Both content caches are self-healing: a failure or disabled-by-flag placeholder is recognised on the next run and regenerated rather than served. Utils.isRetryableExplanationPlaceholder guards explanations; DocumentGeneratorMain.isRetryablePlaceholder guards examples per-type so only the missing type is regenerated. This is what makes a credential-less first run harmless and removes the need to delete the output directory.

nodes.label: Sanitized rule JSON
nodes.rationale: The HTML-stripped, structured JSON form of a rule written by Java for Python to read as dependency context only. Utils.sanitizeRuleFileSecure strips HTML, expands tooltips, de-duplicates lists, confines I/O under llm/ via enforceUnderBase and caps input at 2 MB. It is the one cache with no invalidation story at all.

nodes.label: Cross-feature hidden dependency - examples need the explanation path
nodes.rationale: Example generation needs llm/sanitized_rules/*.json for cross-rule context, but only getLLMExplanation writes them - getLLMExample does not. Running --llm-explanations=off --llm-examples=on on a clean checkout silently degrades every Dependency Guarantees/Constraints section to (none) with no warning. Worked around by documentation rather than code; the real fix moves the sanitize step out of the explanation path so both consumers trigger it.

nodes.label: Naming inversion in the dependency-graph code
nodes.rationale: ensuresToRequiresMap actually holds providers and requiresToEnsuresMap holds consumers, and the call site passes them into parameters named the other way round. The two inversions cancel out so the rendered trees are correct today, but naively 'fixing' the argument order to match the parameter names would silently swap the trees on every page. Any fix must rename variables and parameters together in one change with a rendered-output diff.

nodes.label: Deliberate absence of a concurrency model
nodes.rationale: Zero threads, executors, parallel streams or synchronization in Java; zero threading, asyncio or multiprocessing in Python. Subprocesses are spawned strictly one at a time and blocked on. Landmine for future parallelization: Order.java keeps three static fields as per-rule scratch space cleared in a finally block, safe only because rules are processed sequentially. Idempotency is cache-based, not transactional - a run killed mid-write leaves partial files and a rerun resumes from there.

nodes.label: Error-handling philosophy by layer
nodes.rationale: Three incompatible styles coexist: CLI parsing exits 255 (clear interactively, but makes DocSettings impossible to unit test or embed); rule loading batches then falls back per file and continues; sentence generation throws upward uncaught; graph verification throws a production assertion; Java-side LLM failures become page content instead of aborting; and cache writes swallow IOException deliberately - the one clearly justified swallow in the codebase. No top-level handler wraps main.

nodes.label: Measured runtime across backends
nodes.rationale: --llm=off completes in 1.23 s, so effectively 100% of an LLM run is enrichment and optimising Tier 1 or Tier 3 would be wasted effort. Runtime is not driven by rate limiting - under 0.3% of gateway wall-clock. Rule complexity is a poor predictor: the 144-line Cipher produced one of the fastest example times while the 25-line IvParameterSpec took 70 s. The dominant variable is how many compile-repair rounds burn, which is model- and run-specific.

nodes.label: Test coverage gap
nodes.rationale: Seven tests, roughly 40 lines of coverage against 8,922 lines of Java and 3,628 of Python, with no CI pipeline. Untested and highest-risk: the twelve sentence generators, Order.java's regex parser, the graph algorithms, the JSON sanitizer, the rule-to-page pairing, and all Python prompt shaping. The pairing case is the argument: it broke in production, went unnoticed across 51 pages and an archived release, and a two-rule golden-output fixture would have caught it on the introducing commit.

nodes.label: Dead and unused code inventory
nodes.rationale: Still dead: StringEncryption, header.ftl, Utils.extract (orphaned once its sole caller was deleted), two CrySLReader loaders, FunctionUtils.getEventNames, ComposedRule.methods, nine template data-model keys the template never reads, and the Maven unpack-ruleset step. Also declared-but-unused slf4j/logback (no logger is ever instantiated - all output is System.out/err) against used-but-undeclared commons-io and javax.servlet-api arriving purely transitively. No LICENSE file exists.

nodes.label: CLI reference and flag grammar
nodes.rationale: Only --reportPath is mandatory, and it also roots both LLM cache directories. Toggle flags are switches that flip a default true to false. Flags parse left to right with later ones overriding earlier; any unrecognised flag prints usage and exits 255. The --llm= value grammar originally treated anything not off/false/0 as ON, so --llm=disable silently enabled the feature - now strictly validated.

nodes.label: Codebase-side environment variable table
nodes.rationale: The same variables the README documents for operators, but annotated with the source location that reads each one - llm_code_writer_secure.py for the compile-gate and repair budget, LLMService.buildCompileClasspath for the classpath hatches, LLMService:142-144 for the sidecar timeouts, LLMService.resolveJavacBinary for JAVAC_BIN.

nodes.label: redirectErrorStream merges Python stderr into the answer
nodes.rationale: ProcessBuilder.redirectErrorStream(true) merges each subprocess's stderr into the stream Java treats as its answer. The code-example path filters this out via fenced-code-block extraction; the explanation path does not, so stray [WARN]/[INFO] lines from Python can be cached and rendered directly into the documentation.

nodes.label: Unsanitized client-side rendering of LLM output
nodes.rationale: Generated pages call container.innerHTML = marked.parse(container.textContent) on cached LLM text, and marked does not sanitize, so anything in the cache becomes live HTML in the reader's browser. Blast radius is limited because pages are local static files - but the tool is explicitly designed to produce distributable documentation via --booleanF.

nodes.label: CDN-only client dependencies with no offline fallback
nodes.rationale: Every generated page loads d3 5.16, @hpcc-js/wasm and d3-graphviz from unpkg and marked (unpinned) from jsdelivr, both render-critical with no offline fallback. Offline the diagram never renders and explanations show raw markdown source; only the collapsible sections survive, since that logic has no external dependency.

nodes.label: Generated site client-side behaviour
nodes.rationale: All interactivity is plain inline JavaScript in singleclass.ftl with no build step and no framework: collapsible sections, recursive FreeMarker macros rendering requires/ensures trees into nested lists, a client-side d3-graphviz render of the DOT string, a language switcher that lazily marked-parses each explanation once (guarded by data-rendered), copy buttons, and a substring sidebar filter.

nodes.label: de.upb.userstudy.StringEncryption
nodes.rationale: A standalone demo class with its own main and no callers in the pipeline, retained because git history shows it was a deliberate user-study artifact. It is compiled into the shipped JAR, which is what turned dead code into a distributable liability.

nodes.label: Working-directory dependency of the LLM sidecar
nodes.rationale: LLMService.PROJECT_ROOT is user.dir and every script path is relative, so LLM features only work when the JVM is launched from the repository root; running the JAR elsewhere makes every subprocess spawn fail to find its script and surfaces as generic failure placeholders. The venv is looked for at <repo_root>/.venv only, despite .gitignore still listing llm/.venv/.

nodes.label: Known issues register
nodes.rationale: Split into Still open and Fixed, cross-referenced against AUDIT.md's finding IDs so the codebase reference and the audit history stay reconciled rather than drifting into two accounts of the same defects.
